samples.result:
# On the Slow Work of Noticing

I am sitting on the porch of a rented cabin in the Catskills, and the morning is doing something unspeakably ordinary: it is arriving. The light has not yet cleared the ridge, so the valley below is a bowl of gray-blue mist, and the grass is wet in a way that only grass can be wet before the sun has had a chance to argue with it. There is a bird—I cannot name it, though I should be able to—repeating the same three notes over and over, as if it is testing the quality of the air. The coffee in my hands is hot. There is no hurry.

I have not written freely like this in a long time. Not because I lack words, but because I have come to distrust the conditions under which words are usually produced. Most of my writing these days is squeezed into small gaps between notifications, or built out of fragments harvested while waiting for a meeting to start, or typed while half-listening to a podcast about the end of the world. The writing that matters—the kind that changes you, that makes you look up from the page as if you had just realized you were being watched—requires a different kind of climate. It requires boredom, slowness, a willingness to sit with the blankness of the page until the page stops being blank. It requires, in short, the thing that the modern world has made almost impossible: a sustained period of undirected attention.

This is what I have been trying to think about, in the loose and undistinguished way that one thinks about things before one is ready to write them: attention. Not the kind of attention that is measured by analytics, or the kind that is bought and sold by advertisers, or the kind that is constantly being optimized and gamified by the designers of the apps we are ashamed to be scrolling through. I mean the older, slower, more dangerous kind. The kind that is almost indistinguishable from love. The kind that, when you give it to something, you are quietly saying: you are worthy of my time, and time is the only thing I truly have.

There is a phrase often attributed to the French philosopher Simone Weil, though it is more of a distillation than a direct quote: “Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.” I used to read that as a nice sentiment, a bit of mystical wisdom to be admired and then put aside. Now I think it is one of the most profound and practically important statements that has ever been made about how to live. Because attention is not just a cognitive act. It is not merely a matter of directing your eyes or your ears toward something. It is a moral act. It is a way of allowing the world to be real outside of your own need for it. When you pay attention to a person, you are not just listening to their words; you are creating a space in which their existence becomes undeniable. When you pay attention to a landscape, you are not just looking at it; you are entering into a relationship with it, one in which you are not the center.

And when you pay attention to a single, small, seemingly insignificant thing—a bird repeating three notes, a blade of grass, the particular way the light falls on a wooden table—you are doing something quietly revolutionary. You are resisting the pull of the abstract, the spectacular, the catastrophic. You are saying that the world is not just a set of data points to be processed and discarded, but a dense, textured, infinite field of meaning. You are saying that the small is not the enemy of the large, but its foundation.

# II

I did not come to these thoughts by accident. I came to them by walking.

A few years ago, I moved to a new city, and I began a practice that I have kept ever since: I started walking the same route every morning, at the same time, regardless of weather. The route is not long—about two miles, down a residential street, past a small park, across a bridge over a creek, and then back along a different road. It is not a scenic route, strictly speaking. There is no dramatic vista, no ocean, no mountain range. Just houses, lawns, cars, a few trees, a gas station, a convenience store, and the creek, which in the dry season is little more than a trickle of mud and stones.

At first, the walk was boring. I would put in earbuds and listen to something—a book, a podcast, a playlist—to fill the silence. But after a while, the earbuds began to irritate me, and I took them out. And what I discovered was that the walk was not actually boring at all. It was just that I had never bothered to look at it.

The first thing I noticed was the dogs. There is a golden retriever who lives in the blue house on the corner, and every morning she is standing at the gate, watching the street with the serene patience of a creature who has never once questioned the usefulness of her own existence. There is a small, wiry terrier who is walked by an old man in a flannel shirt, and the terrier stops at exactly the same fire hydrant every day, sniffs it for precisely eleven seconds, and then moves on. There is a black lab who has learned to lie in the sun on the driveway of the house with the red door, and when I pass by, he lifts his head and looks at me with an expression that seems to say: *If you were me, you would not be in such a hurry.*

Then I noticed the plants. There is a particular hedge of azaleas that blooms in mid-May, and one year I watched it go from tight green buds to a riot of pink in the span of a single week. There is a magnolia tree in the park that loses its leaves all at once in the autumn, and the sound of the leaves hitting the ground is like the sound of a great hand gently exhaling. There is a patch of wild mint that grows along the creek, and when I crush a leaf between my fingers, the smell is so sharp and clean that it feels like a memory of something I have never experienced.

And then I noticed the light. The way it changes, not just from season to season, but from day to day, minute to minute. Sometimes the morning light is pale and watery, as if the world were being viewed through the bottom of a glass. Sometimes it is golden and thick, like honey being poured over the rooftops. Sometimes it is gray and flat, and the houses look like they are carved from the same stone as the sky. I began to understand that the walk was never really the same walk. It was always a new walk, wearing the clothes of the old one. And the only reason it had seemed repetitive was that I had not been paying attention.

This is the first lesson of the slow work of noticing: repetition is not monotony. It is invitation. The same route, walked a hundred times, is a hundred different routes. But you can only see the difference if you are willing to be bored, to be empty, to let the world speak instead of always trying to speak at it.

# III

There is a reason why the digital economy is built on the destruction of this capacity. Attention is the raw material of almost everything in our age—advertising, politics, culture, even friendship. And the most reliable way to extract value from attention is to fragment it, to keep it moving, to never allow it to settle. The scroll is the perfect technology for this. It presents an infinite series of small, novel, mildly interesting things, none of which requires more than a moment of engagement. The scroll is not a tool for reading. It is a tool for avoiding the possibility of reading, for avoiding the possibility of any sustained encounter with a single thing that might demand something from you.

I have spent hours of my life scrolling. I have spent hours of my life watching videos that I do not remember, reading articles that I could not summarize, absorbing information that vanished from my mind the moment it entered it. And I have noticed, in myself, a strange new symptom: the inability to sit with a thought without immediately reaching for my phone. It is not that I have something to say or something to check. It is that the silence of my own mind has become uncomfortable. It is that the sensation of having only my own thoughts for company feels like a kind of withdrawal.

This is not a new insight. Every critic of the modern age, from Nicholas Carr to Jenny Odell to Mary Oliver, has pointed out the same thing. But the insight bears repeating, because the experience does not get less urgent, the more it is described. There is a kind of poverty that is invisible to the people who suffer from it, and that poverty is the poverty of attention. You can have a full bank account, a full refrigerator, a full calendar, and still be starving—starving for silence, starving for depth, starving for the feeling of being fully present in a single moment, in a single place, with a single other being.

The strange thing is that the tools that promised to connect us have made us less capable of connection. Because connection requires attention, and attention requires time, and time requires the willingness to let a relationship unfold at its own pace, without interruption, without optimization, without the constant sense that there might be something better, shinier, more immediate just around the corner. When you are with someone and you are checking your phone, you are not really with them. You are with the phone, and the phone is with everyone else. And the person in front of you knows it—not always consciously, but in the way that a plant knows the direction of the light. They know that they are only partially receiving your attention, and that partial attention is not the same as attention. It is the shadow of attention. It is attention with one foot out the door.

# IV

I have often wondered whether the slow work of noticing can be taught, or whether it is just a temperament that some people have and others do not. I have come to believe that it is a practice, not a personality trait. And like all practices, it requires a kind of discipline—but not the discipline of forcing yourself to do something you hate. The discipline of removing the obstacles that prevent you from doing what you love. The discipline of putting the phone in another room. The discipline of taking the earbuds out. The discipline of walking the same route and not getting bored. The discipline of being with your own thoughts even when they are not interesting, because it is only in the boring, empty, unfocused spaces that interesting thoughts have room to grow.

I wonder if this is why so many of my best ideas have come to me in the shower, or while washing dishes, or while doing some other repetitive, mindless task. It is not because the shower is a magical place. It is because the shower is one of the few remaining places where I am not being stimulated, where my attention is not being captured, where my mind is free to wander. And a wandering mind is not a wasted mind. A wandering mind is a mind that is making connections, that is sorting memories, that is weaving together disparate threads into new patterns. The problem with the constant stimulus of the digital world is not that it fills our minds with bad content. It is that it fills our minds with any content at all. It leaves no room for the spontaneous, the unexpected, the unbidden. It leaves no room for surprise.

The slow work of noticing is the work of making room for surprise. It is the work of going to the same place every day and letting that place become new. It is the work of reading a single poem ten times and discovering, on the tenth reading, that you had never really read it before. It is the work of sitting with a person you love and not checking your phone, not because you are trying to be good, but because you have realized that the phone is a thief, and you have decided that you do not want to be robbed anymore.

# V

There is a specific kind of attention that I want to practice, and it is the kind that is directed at the non-human world. I have been walking the same route for years, and I have come to know it the way that one knows an old friend—not just its broad outlines, but its moods, its quirks, its small daily changes. I know which house puts out a Christmas wreath in early November and leaves it up until March. I know which dog barks at the mailman and which one just watches silently. I know where the sidewalk is cracked and where the roots of the maple tree have lifted the pavement. I know when the light hits the window of the yellow house at a certain angle, and the whole house glows like it is made of amber.

This knowledge is useless in any economic sense. It cannot be monetized. It cannot be turned into a metric or a bullet point on a resume. It is a kind of knowledge that is valuable simply because it makes the world more real. When you know a place this intimately, you cannot treat it as a backdrop for your own drama. You cannot see it as just a scenery, just a resource, just a place to get from A to B. It becomes a presence, an organism, a community of living things of which you are a part. And this, I think, is the deepest purpose of attention: not to master the world, but to be in relationship with it. To notice the crow that sits on the same telephone wire every afternoon, and to wonder, briefly, what it is thinking. To notice the first frost on the grass, and to feel not just the cold, but the passage of time. To notice the way the creek changes after a rain, swollen and brown and impatient, and to understand that you are living in a world that is always moving, always changing, always becoming something other than what it was.

In one of her notebooks, the poet Mary Oliver wrote: “Attention is the beginning of devotion.” I think this is exactly right. Devotion is usually imagined as a grand, sweeping thing—a commitment to a cause, a person, a god. But the most enduring devotions are built out of small, repeated acts of attention. The daily walk. The daily prayer. The daily practice of sitting down at the desk and writing, even when you have nothing to say. The daily choice to look at the person you love and actually see them. These are the bricks of a life. And if you do not pay attention to the bricks, the life will be hollow, no matter how grand its architecture.

# VI

I have been writing this essay for several days now, and I have noticed that the act of writing about attention has changed the way I pay attention. I am more aware of the texture of things. The grain of the wood on this desk. The sound of the refrigerator humming in the next room. The weight of the coffee cup in my hand. I am more aware of the time, of the way it passes, of the fact that I will not live forever, and that every moment I spend not paying attention is a moment I have spent as if I were already dead.

This is the terrifying thing about the slow work of noticing: it forces you to confront the fact that your life is finite. If you are constantly distracted, constantly skimming the surface of experience, you can avoid this confrontation. You can pretend that there will always be more time, more chances, more moments. But when you slow down and pay attention, you realize that each moment is irreplaceable. This particular morning, with this particular light, this particular bird, this particular silence—it will never happen again. And the only way to honor it is to be present for it, to let it in, to allow it to become part of you.

There is a line from the poet Rainer Maria Rilke that I have carried with me for years, from his *Letters to a Young Poet*: “Have patience with everything unresolved in your heart and try to love the questions themselves.” I used to think of this as good advice for a young person, for someone who was struggling with uncertainty. But now I think it is also good advice for the practice of attention. The world is full of questions. Why does the light do that? Why does the bird sing those three notes? Why does this moment feel so full, so heavy, so significant, when nothing is happening at all? You do not need to answer them. You just need to let them be, to sit with them, to let them deepen. The answer, if there is one, will come in its own time. Or it will not. And that is also fine.

# VII

It is now late afternoon. The light has shifted again, and the valley is no longer full of mist. The bird is gone, or has fallen silent. The coffee is long since finished. I have been sitting here for hours, doing nothing in particular, and I have come to a strange conclusion: this is the work. This is the real work. Not the writing, not the thinking, not the producing of something that can be measured or shared or consumed. The real work is the paying attention. The writing is just a byproduct, a way of recording the attention, of making it last a little longer.

I think about the people who will read this, if anyone does. I hope they will not read it as a set of instructions. I hope they will not read it as a criticism of their own habits, a judgment of their own distractedness. I hope they will read it as an invitation. An invitation to take a walk without your phone. An invitation to sit in silence for five minutes and see what comes. An invitation to notice the small things, the overlooked things, the things that seem too ordinary to be worth your time. Because they are not too ordinary. They are the only things that are real.

The world is enormous, and it is mostly made of tiny, unremarkable things. A blade of grass. A drop of water. A single note from a bird. The way a stranger’s face changes when they smile. These are not distractions from the important work of life. They are the important work. They are the texture of existence, the very fabric of being. And the slow work of noticing is the work of weaving yourself into that fabric, of becoming a part of it, of understanding that you are not a separate observer but a participant, a thread, a small and temporary piece of a vast and ancient pattern.

I am going to go for another walk now. The same route as always. The same street, the same houses, the same creek, the same dogs, the same trees. And I know, with a certainty that I cannot explain, that it will not be the same at all.

You asked me to write freely about whatever I want, so I will take you at your word. There is something mildly terrifying about a blank page even when the task is simple, especially when you have been given permission to say anything. The blank page is not actually blank; it is a field of infinite possibility, and infinity has a way of making a finite mind feel small. So I will do what writers have always done when confronted with openness: I will pick a small door and open it, and hope that what lies behind is a hallway worth walking down.

I am sitting in a café right now, or at least I am imagining a café, because the act of writing is always an act of imagination, even when you are describing the chair you are sitting in. Let me make the café real. There is a low winter sun coming through the window, casting long shadows across a wooden table. There is a mug in front of me, the coffee gone cold, because I have been staring at this laptop for longer than I intended. There is a couple at the next table arguing quietly about something that neither of them will remember next week. There is a barista with tattoos up both arms, steaming milk in a metallic pitcher, the hiss of steam like a distant curtain. There is a smell of roasted beans and rain. I notice all these things because I am trying to notice them, which is itself a strange way to move through the world. Most of the time, we do not notice anything. We see a blur of shapes and colors, and our brains fill in the gaps with expectations. We are not experiencing the world; we are reading a heavily edited summary of it. People say that wisdom comes from experience, but truly it comes from paying attention to experience. A hundred years of life lived in a haze is not a hundred years; it is one year repeated a hundred times, with different wallpaper.

Attention is a strange faculty. The Latin root is *attendere*, which means to stretch toward, to reach out. Attention is a kind of reaching. When you pay attention to a person, you are literally extending yourself toward them, across the space between two bodies. When you pay attention to a tree, you are crossing the boundary between human and nonhuman, at least for a moment. Attention is the most basic form of love. It is also the most scarce resource in the modern world. We live in an economy that has learned to harvest attention the way we harvest oil, by drilling into the soft ground of our minds and pumping out whatever is liquid. The devices in our pockets are not tools; they are extraction machines. Every notification is a tiny fishing hook. Every infinite scroll is a conveyor belt. The most successful companies of our time are not selling products; they are selling your focus, in fractions of a second, to advertisers who have learned to speak in the language of your anxieties. The irony is that we call this “social media,” when it is often the most isolating thing ever built. We sit alone in our rooms, watching strangers perform their lives, while the people in the same room as us become increasingly abstract.

I have been trying to understand what happens to the mind when it is constantly interrupted. There is a kind of mental churn that feels like productivity but is actually just the sound of a brain switching tasks without ever completing any of them. I open a document to write. I get an email. I check the email, then I check the news, then I check the weather, then I remember the email, then I open a new tab to research something unrelated, then I forget why I opened the tab. Then I look out the window and see a bird, and for a moment I am saved. The bird is doing nothing except being a bird. It is not interrupted. It is not multitasking. It is simply alive, and its attention is exactly where it needs to be, on the branch, on the seed, on the wind. I envy the bird. I have read that the average attention span in the early 2000s was about twelve seconds, and that it has since fallen to eight seconds, which is supposedly shorter than a goldfish’s. I do not fully believe these statistics, because they were popularized by an advertising agency and have been repeated uncritically for years. But even if the numbers are nonsense, the feeling is real. I can sit through a three-hour movie without checking my phone, but I cannot read a single page of a dense book without my hand twitching toward the screen. The twitch is learned. It is a conditioned reflex, like Pavlov’s dog, except the bell is a notification and the drool is a dopamine release.

And yet I do not want to write a simple lament about technology, because technology is not a villain. It is a mirror. It magnifies what is already inside us. If we are distracted, it is because we have not learned to be present. If we are anxious, it is because we have not learned to be calm. If we are superficial, it is because we have not learned to be deep. The phone is not the problem; the problem is that we have outsourced our inner lives to external stimuli and then blamed the stimuli for being stimulating. I remember the first time I took a walk without my phone. I had read somewhere that this was good for you, like taking vitamins or flossing. I walked down the street, and for the first ten minutes I felt a phantom buzzing in my pocket. My hand kept reaching for something that was not there. My mind kept wandering to imaginary messages. Then, slowly, something strange happened. The street began to appear. I noticed the way the light fell on a brick wall. I noticed the sound of a bicycle bell, the smell of a bakery, the texture of a cracked sidewalk. It was as if I had been living in a house with the curtains drawn, and someone had finally opened them. The world was not boring. The world was beautiful, ridiculously beautiful, but I had been too busy staring at a glowing rectangle to see it.

This is the paradox of the modern age: we are more connected than any humans in history, yet more alone. We have access to the sum total of human knowledge, yet we use it to read about the hobbies of celebrities. We can talk to anyone anywhere on Earth, yet we sit in silence across the table from our families. I do not mean to moralize. I am as guilty as anyone. But I have come to believe that the antidote to distraction is not discipline; it is wonder. You cannot force yourself to pay attention through sheer willpower for long. Willpower is a finite battery that depletes by the hour. But wonder is self-renewing. When you are truly curious, attention becomes effortless. You do not need to tell yourself to look; you cannot help but look. The problem is that we have trained ourselves to be curious about the wrong things. We are curious about what our friends ate for breakfast, about the latest scandal, about the next episode of a show we do not even like. We have become connoisseurs of the trivial. Meanwhile, the deep mysteries of existence—the nature of consciousness, the origin of the universe, the face of the person we love—sit unvisited, like a library nobody enters.

I once spent a summer on the coast of Maine, in a town so small that the post office was also the grocery store and the hardware store. I was there to write, but I spent most of my time walking. Every day, at low tide, I would go down to the rocky shore and look at the tide pools. These pools are like tiny worlds. In one, you can see a hermit crab dragging its borrowed shell across a bed of green algae. In another, a starfish clings to a rock, motionless, as if it has decided to become part of the geology. In a third, there is a transparent shrimp, almost invisible, darting between shadows. I could spend an hour at a single pool, and I often did. The locals probably thought I was strange, a grown man crouching in the cold wind, staring at water. But I was not staring. I was entering. The pool was a lens, and through it I could see the whole history of life on Earth, the endless experiment of evolution, the strange miracle of creatures that have no brains but still manage to eat and move and reproduce. There is a phrase in Zen: “When you sit, just sit. When you walk, just walk.” I had read it many times, but I never understood it until I crouched beside a tide pool. The water was cold. The wind was sharp. The only thing in the world was the pool. And for a few minutes, I was not in my head. I was not thinking about the past or the future. I was not planning, regretting, or wanting. I was just there, stretched toward the water, attending.

That feeling is hard to sustain. The mind wanders. It always wanders. But I have learned that wandering is not the enemy. In fact, some of my best ideas have come when I was not paying attention to anything in particular. There is a distinction between focused attention and diffuse attention. Focused attention is like a spotlight; it illuminates a small area with great intensity. Diffuse attention is like a lantern; it illuminates a wide area with less intensity. Creativity seems to require both. You need the spotlight to understand a problem deeply, to read, to analyze, to practice. But you need the lantern to connect disparate ideas, to see patterns, to have those sudden “Aha!” moments in the shower. The shower is a classic example. You are not thinking about the problem. Your mind is loose, drifting, free. And then the solution arrives, seemingly from nowhere, like a fish that jumps out of the water. This is not magic. It is what happens when your brain continues to work in the background, integrating information that your conscious mind has been chewing on. But this background process cannot happen if you never let your mind be background. If you are constantly stimulated, constantly scrolling, constantly filling every silence with noise, the lantern never gets to glow. The diffuse mode never gets a chance. You are all spotlight, all the time, and the spotlight burns out.

I think about this when I write. Writing is a strange act. It requires enormous concentration, but it also requires a kind of surrender. You sit down with an idea, but the idea is not a finished thing. It is a seed. You have to water it, but you also have to let it grow on its own, in its own direction. If you try to control every word, the prose becomes stiff, wooden, dead. If you let go completely, the prose becomes shapeless, rambling, obscure. The art is in the balance. You attend to the sentence, but you also attend to the silence between sentences, the white space, the rhythm. You listen to the words as much as you speak them. This is why writing is exhausting. It is a form of paying attention that goes beyond the normal. You are paying attention to something that does not exist yet. You are trying to bring it into being through sheer focus. And sometimes, if you are lucky, you get into a flow state. Time disappears. The room disappears. You are just a channel, a conduit, something through which language is flowing. It is the closest I have come to religious experience. It is also terribly fragile. A single notification can break the spell, and then you are back in the room, blinking at the screen, wondering where you went.

I have been thinking a lot about language and attention. Words are how we slice reality. Every language has a different set of knives. In English, we have one word for snow, but the Inuit languages have many, because snow is a matter of survival, and you need to distinguish between the snow that is good for building an igloo and the snow that is good for hunting and the snow that is dangerous to walk on. This does not mean that English speakers cannot see the different kinds of snow; we can. But we have to work harder to notice them, because our language does not hand us the categories. The same is true for emotions. English has a relatively small vocabulary for feelings. We say “sad” and “happy” and “angry,” but these are broad buckets. Other languages have words for specific shades of feeling, like the Japanese word *mono no aware*, which means the gentle sadness of impermanence, the beauty of things passing. Or the Portuguese word *saudade*, which is a longing for something that may never return. Or the German word *Fernweh*, which is a homesickness for places you have never been. When we learn these words, our attention expands. We begin to notice experiences that we previously ignored because we had no name for them. Language is not just a tool for communication; it is a tool for perception. It shapes what we see, what we feel, what we remember.

Poetry is the art of using language to sharpen attention. A poem is a compression. It takes a complex experience and squeezes it into a few lines, so that every word is load-bearing. When you read a poem slowly, you are forced to slow down. You cannot skim a poem the way you skim a tweet. You have to pause, re-read, sound out the words. The poet has arranged the sounds and the rhythms and the meanings in such a way that the poem demands your presence. I remember the first time I read T.S. Eliot’s “The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock.” I was in college, lying on a threadbare couch, and I read the opening lines:

*Let us go then, you and I,*

*When the evening is spread out against the sky*

*Like a patient etherized upon a table;*

I have never forgotten those lines, not because I have a good memory, but because they stopped me. The image of the evening as a patient etherized upon a table is so strange and precise that it rearranged something in my mind. I had seen many evenings. I had seen sunsets and twilight. But I had never seen an evening as something anesthetized, something helpless, something suspended between life and death. The poem gave me a new way to look at the sky. It expanded my attention.

I wonder if the decline of poetry in our culture is actually a decline in the capacity for attention. We have replaced poems with memes, which are also compressed, but in a different way. A meme is a shortcut. It is designed to be consumed in a second and then discarded. It gives you a quick hit of recognition—the same joke, the same format, the same reaction—and then it vanishes into the feed, replaced by another meme, and another. This is not necessarily bad. Memes are a form of social glue. They create shared references and a sense of belonging. But they train the brain to expect constant novelty, constant stimulation, constant payoff. They make it harder to sit with something difficult, something that does not immediately reward you. A poem asks you to work. A novel asks you to invest hours. A long essay asks you to hold multiple ideas in your head at once. These are muscles. If you do not exercise them, they atrophy. And then you find yourself unable to read anything longer than a paragraph, unable to follow an argument, unable to sit in silence with your own thoughts. I do not want that for myself. I do not want it for anyone.

But I also do not want to be a Luddite. Technology has done wonderful things. It has brought us music, medicine, and the ability to talk to loved ones across oceans. It has helped me write this essay, which will be delivered to you through channels that would have seemed like magic a century ago. The question is not how to get rid of technology; the question is how to use it without being used. As the philosopher Ivan Illich said, tools should be convivial; they should extend our freedom, not diminish it. A hammer is convivial. It amplifies the strength of your arm, but it does not tell you what to build. A smartphone, as it is currently designed, is not convivial. It is a slot machine. It is a casino in your pocket, with a thousand games and a thousand bells and a thousand ways to lose your time. But you can make it more convivial. You can turn off notifications. You can delete the apps that feed on your attention. You can set boundaries. You can use it as a tool instead of as a master. This is not easy. The systems are designed to be addictive. But it is possible. The first step is to notice. The second step is to choose.

I think about attention not just as a personal matter but as a political and ethical one. Who gets your attention is a moral question. The media companies that decide which stories to cover are making decisions about what is visible and what is invisible. A child starving in Yemen is invisible if the camera does not go there. A village flooded by a rising sea is invisible if the algorithm does not surface it. Our attention is finite. When we spend it on trivialities, we are not spending it on what matters. But it is not enough to say that we should pay attention to what matters. We also have to decide what matters, and that is a difficult and contested question. Perhaps the answer is that everything matters, but not equally, and the act of ranking is the act of living. Every time you choose to look at something, you are choosing not to look at something else. This is the tragedy of attention. It is a form of sacrifice. To pay attention to the person in front of you, you must let go of the crowd. To pay attention to a book, you must close the browser. To pay attention to the present moment, you must stop dwelling on the past or worrying about the future. This is hard. It is hard because we want to hold everything, to keep all options open, to be everywhere at once. But we cannot. We are finite creatures. Our attention is finite. Our time is finite. The only wisdom is to spend that finitude well.

I have a friend who is a hospice nurse. She told me that when people are dying, they rarely talk about their accomplishments. They talk about the people they loved and the people who loved them. They talk about moments of beauty, a sunset, a song, a child’s laugh. They talk about the things they paid attention to. No one says, on their deathbed, “I wish I had spent more time looking at my phone.” No one says, “I wish I had checked my email more often.” They say, “I wish I had spent more time with my family.” “I wish I had told her I loved her.” “I wish I had slowed down.” These are all statements about attention. To love someone is to pay attention to them. To regret not loving someone is to regret not paying attention to them. The end of life is a great clarifier. It strips away the noise. It reveals what was always important. But we do not have to wait until the end to know this. We can know it now. We can choose, every day, to stretch ourselves toward what matters.

I am back in the café, the coffee cold, the sun lower in the sky. The couple at the next table has stopped arguing. They are holding hands, silently. The barista has turned on some music, something slow and acoustic. Outside, people walk by with their heads down, their faces lit by the pale glow of screens. Inside, I am writing to you, and you are reading this, and in some strange way we are paying attention to each other across the void of time and space. This is a miracle, if you think about it. Language, moving from mind to mind, surviving the distance, evoking images and feelings in a brain that is not my own. That is all any of us can do: to reach out, to attend, to make something that another soul can hold. The essay is almost done. It has wandered, as I promised it would. But maybe it has not wandered aimlessly. Maybe it has been circling a single point, the way a hawk circles a field. The point is this: attention is the thread that connects us to everything. It is the substance of love, the medium of art, the engine of understanding. Guard it. Use it. Spend it on things that deserve it. And when you find yourself lost in the noise, come back to the simplest act: look at something, really look, and let it be enough.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
It begins with a threshold. The front door, the gate, the edge of the doormat where the inside becomes the outside. There is a particular moment — pregnant, suspended — when you have not yet begun, when the body is still a domestic object, a piece of furniture with a pulse. Then your foot crosses the line, and the world takes you. Every walk is a kind of birth. You emerge, blinking, into a space that cares nothing for your appointments or your anxieties, and for a little while you are nothing more than a moving point, a consciousness attached to a pair of shoes.

I have been walking for as long as I can remember, though I did not always know it. As a child, walking was simply a pedestrian way of getting from one place to another, a mode of locomotion that adults seemed to treat with suspicion when it was not strictly necessary. The word "walk" itself carried a disciplinary weight: you walked to school because you had to, you walked the dog because the dog required it, and in the summer you walked to the pool, your feet slapping hot asphalt, the taste of sunscreen on your lips. Nobody told me that walking was also a way of thinking, of dreaming, of being alone in the company of the world. That discovery came later, and it came the way most discoveries do: by accident.

I remember the exact street. I was sixteen, maybe seventeen, and I had just lived through one of those adolescent devastations that feel like the end of the world but are really just the beginning of its education. A friendship had fractured. A crush had gone unrequited. Nothing catastrophic by adult standards, but at the time it was a sufficient catastrophe. I did not know what to do with the feelings. They were too large for my bedroom, too loud for my headphones. So I did the only thing that suggested itself: I left the house, and I walked.

I walked without destination, down streets I had known since childhood but had never really seen. The houses were familiar; their details were not. I noticed the way a certain kind of blue paint flaked on a particular porch, how a fence that I had passed a thousand times was actually made of two different kinds of wood, the strange geography of shadows in the late afternoon. I noticed the rhythm. My feet hit the pavement in a regular cadence — left, right, left, right — and my breath synced to it, and my thoughts, which had been a tangled knot, began to loosen, strand by strand. By the time I came home, an hour later, something had rearranged itself inside me. Not fixed, not resolved, but rearranged. The world had made room for my unhappiness by being bigger than it, and walking was the way I slipped into that largeness.

That is, I think, the secret of walking. It is the one human activity that combines the physical and the mental in perfect balance, that lets the body do its ancient work while the mind is free to wander, drift, solve, or simply be. There is a reason the Greek philosophers were called Peripatetics — they taught while walking. There is a reason Nietzsche claimed that all truly great thoughts are conceived while walking. There is a reason that the act of pacing is so synonymous with thinking that we do it even in small rooms, even in our own heads. The body knows what the mind needs. It knows that forward motion is a kind of permission to think forward, that the rhythm of the feet is a metronome for the soul.

I have walked in many places. I have walked the long, straight streets of Midwestern towns, where the horizon is a rumor and the sidewalks are endless. I have walked the narrow, winding paths of European cities, where every corner is a memory and every alley smells of coffee and stone. I have walked in the mountains, where the air is thin and the silence is vast, and I have walked along the ocean, where the water writes and erases its own message with every wave. I have walked in the rain, in the snow, in the heat of deserts where even the cactus seemed to be sweating, and in the cold of northern winters where my breath froze in the air like a ghost I was exhaling.

But the walking I return to, the walking that feels most like thinking, is the walking of the suburban night. There is a particular quality to the hour after midnight in a residential neighborhood. The houses are dark, or nearly so, lit by the blue glow of televisions behind curtains. The streets are empty. The cars are parked, all of them, in the driveways and along the curbs, like sleeping animals. The streetlights cast pools of yellow light, and between them, there are pools of shadow. The world is quiet in a way it never is during the day — not silent, but quiet, a hum of distant highway and the occasional bark of a dog, the rustle of a cat in the bushes. In this quiet, you become aware of your own footsteps. They are loud. They are the only sound you are making, and they seem to be making you as well. Step by step, you are assembling yourself out of the night.

I have had some of my best thoughts on those walks. Not the kind of thoughts that solve problems, necessarily, but the kind that open windows. I have arrived at insights about my own life that had been hiding in plain sight, waiting for the right pace to reveal them. I have remembered dreams I had forgotten, revived arguments I had lost, written poems that I never set down on paper. The night is a generous companion. It asks nothing of you. It does not require you to be cheerful or productive or interesting. It only asks that you keep moving, and in return it gives you time — time that is yours, time that is free, time that is not accountable to anyone.

There is a name for this kind of time. The Japanese call it *stin* — the art of forest bathing, of walking slowly through nature to absorb its atmosphere. The English have a phrase: "taking a constitutional" — a walk taken for health, but really an constitution taken for the soul. The French say *flâner* — to stroll, to saunter, to wander the city without purpose, observing its life. All these traditions understand something that the modern world tries to forget: walking is not merely transportation. It is not merely exercise. It is a way of being, a technology of attention, a method for making the world visible.

Because here is the thing: you do not see the world when you are moving fast. You see it when you are moving slow. At 60 miles per hour, the landscape is a blur, a succession of generalized impressions — trees, buildings, signs — none of them distinct. At 15 miles per hour, on a bicycle, you see a bit more: the texture of a brick wall, the pattern of a garden, the face of a pedestrian at the corner. But at three miles per hour, on foot, you see everything. You see the crack in the sidewalk where a dandelion has pushed through, defiant and improbable. You see the way light falls on a particular window, the way a curtain moves, the shadow of a person inside. You see the small dramas of the world — the ant carrying a crumb, the spider repairing its web, the bird hopping from branch to branch. You see the seasons change, not in the abstract, but in the specific: the first leaf turning, the first frost on a car windshield, the first evening when it is dark at 5 PM and the streetlights come on while the sky is still blue.

This is the gift of walking: it slows the world down to the speed of your attention. And attention, as the poet Mary Oliver famously said, is the beginning of devotion. To walk is to devote yourself to the world, to say to it, "I am here, and I am paying attention." The world rewards this devotion in strange and unexpected ways. It shows you things you would never have seen otherwise. It offers you moments of grace that arrive unbidden — a shaft of light through a canopy of trees, a sound of laughter from a distant porch, a sudden, inexplicable feeling of belonging, as if the streets and the houses and the trees have all agreed to hold you gently, to let you pass through them as if you were their own.

But walking is not always gentle. It can also be hard. I have walked for hours in blizzards, my face numb, my hands buried deep in pockets, and I have asked myself why I was doing it. I have walked through industrial districts where there are no sidewalks, where the trucks roar past and the exhaust stings your eyes, and I have wondered if I was making a mistake. I have walked in places that were dangerous — or at least felt dangerous — where every shadow seemed to hide a threat and every car that slowed seemed to be sizing me up. In those moments, walking stops being a pleasure and becomes a discipline. It becomes an act of will. You keep putting one foot in front of the other because you have decided to, because you are the kind of person who finishes what they start, because there is something in you that needs to arrive, even if you are not sure where you are going.

I have learned, over the years, that this is also part of walking's value. It is a small, portable courage. It is a way of proving to yourself that you can endure. The philosopher Søren Kierkegaard wrote that "above all, do not lose your desire to walk. Every day I walk myself into a state of well-being and walk away from every illness. I have walked myself into my best thoughts, and I know of no thought so burdensome that one cannot walk away from it." Kierkegaard knew something that the psychologists have only recently begun to confirm: movement changes the mind. It changes the chemistry of the brain. It changes the patterns of thought. It is, in a very real sense, a medicine — a medicine that is free, that has no side effects, that can be taken anywhere, at any time, by anyone.

And yet, we have engineered walking out of our lives. The modern world is built for the car, and the car is built for the speed at which you cannot see anything. We have created suburbs without sidewalks, cities without streets for pedestrians, buildings with elevators and parking garages and drive-through windows. We have made walking an anomaly, a hobby, a form of recreation rather than a way of life. We say, "I'm going for a walk," as if it were an event, a special occasion, something that requires planning and appropriate footwear and perhaps a bottle of water. We have forgotten that walking is the original human movement, the thing we did before we did anything else, the thing that carried our ancestors across continents and along coasts and over mountains, the thing that built our bodies and our brains and our cultures.

There is a deep irony in this. The more we have mechanized our movement, the more we have lost touch with our own nature. We are animals. We are walking animals. Our skeletons are built for it, our muscles are built for it, our hearts and lungs are built for it. The human body is a walking machine, and like any machine, it runs best when it is used. When we stop walking, we break ourselves — not just physically, but mentally and spiritually. We become sedentary, static, stuck. We become people who sit in front of screens and forget that there is a world outside the window, a world that is waiting to be witnessed.

I am not saying that walking will solve all your problems. It will not. It will not make you rich or famous or wise. It will not save the world. But it will do something smaller and more important: it will give you yourself back. It will give you your body, which you may have forgotten you had. It will give you your breath, which you may have been holding. It will give you your thoughts, which you may have been suppressing. It will give you the street, the sky, the trees, the neighbors, the dogs, the clouds, the puddles, the cracks in the sidewalk. It will give you all of it, if you are willing to take it, and it will ask only that you keep moving.

I walk almost every day now. Sometimes I walk for ten minutes, just to the corner and back. Sometimes I walk for three hours, out to the edge of town and beyond, along the old farm roads where the pavement gives way to gravel and the gravel gives way to dirt. Sometimes I walk with music, sometimes with a podcast, sometimes in silence. The best walks are the silent ones. In silence, the world speaks. You hear the wind in the power lines, the birds arguing in the trees, the distant sound of a train, the sound of your own breathing, the sound of your own heart. In silence, you can think. You can think about anything. You can think about the people you love and the people you have lost. You can think about the future, about all the possible futures, about the one you are walking toward. You can think about nothing at all, which is perhaps the rarest and most valuable kind of thinking.

There is a particular walk I took last winter that I will not forget. It was a cold, clear night, the kind of night when the stars seem close enough to touch. I had gone out at 11 PM, unable to sleep, restless in that way that only the winter brings. I walked to the edge of my neighborhood, where the streetlights end and the fields begin. The fields were covered in snow, and the snow was glowing under the moon. It was so bright that I could see my shadow, a long, blue shape stretching out behind me. I stood there for a long time, looking at the field, looking at the snow, looking at the moon, and I felt something that I can only describe as a sense of rightness, a sense that everything was exactly as it should be. I was cold. I was tired. I was, in some ways, profoundly lost. But I was also exactly where I was supposed to be, doing exactly what I was supposed to be doing. I was walking. I was alive. I was present. That is enough. That is more than enough.

I think that is what walking ultimately teaches: the art of being present. The present is the only place where you can actually live, and walking is the practice of staying there. When you walk, you cannot be in the past, not really, because the past is behind you, receding with every step. You cannot be in the future, not fully, because the future is ahead of you, and you will not reach it until you arrive. You are in the moment, the only moment, the moment between steps, the moment that is, in some profound sense, all you will ever have.

I remember a line from a novel I read years ago — I cannot recall which one, but the line stayed with me: "We are all walking each other home." That is it. That is what we are doing. We are walking each other home. We are walking our children to school, walking our parents to their graves, walking our friends through their grief, walking strangers through their days. Every walk is a small act of companionship, even when you are walking alone, because you are never truly alone on a walk. You are accompanied by the world. You are accompanied by the memory of everyone who has walked before you, everyone who will walk after you. You are accompanied by your own history, by the person you were when you first learned to walk, by the person you are becoming, step by step.

The great American naturalist John Muir wrote that "in every walk with nature one receives far more than he seeks." I believe this, though I would extend it: in every walk, period, one receives more than one seeks. You set out with a purpose — to get exercise, to clear your head, to reach a destination — and you return with something else. You return with a sight you didn't expect, a thought you didn't have, a feeling you didn't know you were missing. Walking is a gift economy. You give it your time, your effort, your attention, and it gives you back a life.

So I will keep walking. I will keep walking in the morning, when the dew is still on the grass and the world is just waking up. I will keep walking in the afternoon, when the sun is high and the shadows are short and the day feels endless. I will keep walking at night, when the moon is out and the streets are quiet and the thoughts come unbidden. I will walk in the summer, when the heat shimmers off the pavement, and in the winter, when the cold bites at my cheeks. I will walk when I am happy, to celebrate, and when I am sad, to mourn, and when I am confused, to think, and when I am clear, to simply be. I will walk because I can. I will walk because it is what I am built for. I will walk because walking is a way of saying yes to the world, yes to the body, yes to the mind, yes to whatever comes next.

And if you are reading this, I invite you to walk, too. Not because I am telling you to, but because the world is waiting for you. It is waiting outside your door, in the street, in the park, in the fields, in the woods, along the shore. It is waiting with its dandelions and its crack sidewalks, its sunsets and its sunrises, its quiet hours and its loud ones. It is waiting to show you something — something you have not seen, something you have forgotten, something you have always known. It will show you if you are willing to take the first step. It will show you if you are willing to keep going. It will show you, step by step, the way home.

The threshold is still there. The door is still there. The world is still outside, and it is full of walking. It is full of paths and sidewalks and trails and roads, all of them open, all of them waiting. All you have to do is begin. Put on your shoes. Open the door. Cross the line. The first step is the hardest, and it is also the easiest. It is just a step — one small movement, one small act of faith. The rest will follow. It always does.

Walk on.

# The River of Thought: A Meditation on Writing, Freedom, and the Architecture of Mind

There is a particular kind of silence that arrives just before you begin to write. It is not the silence of the room—though that helps—but the silence of the page, that vast white expanse that holds every possibility and no possibility at once. If you sit with it long enough, it begins to hum, like a power line in winter. It is the hum of potential energy, of all the sentences that are about to exist. You could write anything. You could write about the way light falls on a chipped coffee mug at seven in the morning, or about the exact texture of loneliness after a phone call that lasted too long, or about the mathematical elegance of a pinecone, or about the fact that your grandmother once told you that the moon is a hole in the sky. You could write about all of this and more, in any order, in any style, with any degree of coherence. That is the terrifying and exhilarating truth of the blank page: there is no law, no preordained path, no hidden syllabus. There is only you, and the hum, and the words that will or will not come.

And so I begin, not knowing where I am going. This essay is a kind of experiment—an attempt to let the mind wander without a map, to see what it stumbles upon. There is something almost vertiginous about it. When you write without a plan, you are committing to a process of discovery, and discovery is always a little frightening. You are not sure what you will find. You might find something beautiful, or something embarrassing, or something that makes no sense at all. But the finding itself is the point. The river does not ask where it is going; it simply moves, drawn by gravity and the shape of the land. Perhaps I am the river here. Perhaps the land is my own history, my own habits of thought, my own buried memories. Let us see what the river finds.

I am thinking about the word "free." It is a small word, but it carries an enormous weight. We use it to describe everything from political systems to the movement of a bird to the absence of constraints in a creative project. But what does it mean to write freely? It does not mean to write without effort—that would be a kind of nonsense. The great writers, the ones whose prose seems to flow like water, almost always revised obsessively. Freedom is not the absence of constraints; it is the choice of which constraints to embrace. When I write a sonnet, I am not less free than when I write free verse; I am exercising a different kind of freedom, a freedom that is shaped by the very rules I have chosen to follow. There is a beauty in that, a beauty that comes from the tension between the infinite and the finite, between what could be said and what is said within the space of fourteen lines. The blank page is a kind of infinite, but the moment I choose a form, I have voluntarily narrowed it. And yet, in that narrowing, I often find more than I would have in the infinite. The river is free to meander, but it is also shaped by its banks, and it is the banks that give the river its speed and its power.

I think this is why I am so drawn to the practice of free writing—the kind where you simply put pen to paper and do not stop for ten minutes, no matter what comes out. The rules are simple: do not edit, do not judge, do not stop. It is a way of bypassing the inner critic, that harsh voice that tells you that you are not good enough, that you have nothing to say, that this sentence is ugly and that thought is trivial. When you free-write, you are giving yourself permission to be messy. You are allowing the river to flood its banks, to spill over into fields and roads, to carry debris and silt and maybe a few gold flakes along with it. The results are almost always chaotic, but chaos is not the enemy. Chaos is the raw material of meaning. It is the primordial soup from which order emerges, if only you are willing to wait and to watch.

I recall a particular morning, perhaps five years ago, when I decided to free-write for fifteen minutes as a warm-up for a more serious project. I had been feeling blocked, stuck in a loop of self-doubt, unable to produce anything that felt worthy of the time I was spending on it. So I set a timer, took a deep breath, and began to write. What came out was ridiculous. I wrote about the sound of a skateboard on asphalt, about a yellow umbrella I had seen in a gutter, about the fact that I was hungry and could not decide what to eat, about a dream I had had the night before in which I was swimming through a library. I wrote about the color of the sky and the way my left foot was falling asleep and the exact odor of the coffee I was drinking. It was nonsense. But somewhere in the middle of that nonsense, there was a phrase that caught my eye: "the library of the sea." I had written it without thinking, almost as a joke, but as I read it back, I felt a little shiver. It was a beautiful phrase, and it was mine, and it had come out of nowhere. I closed my notebook, stood up, and walked around the room. The phrase stayed with me. It became the seed of a short story about a woman who dives into the ocean to find the books her father had written, books that had been lost when his ship went down. That story would never have existed if I had not allowed myself to write freely, to make a mess, to let the river take me somewhere I had not planned to go.

There is a lesson in that, I think. The unconscious is not a vacuum; it is a vast and teeming ecosystem, full of images, memories, desires, and fears that we do not always have access to in our waking, rational minds. But when we write freely, we are opening a door to that ecosystem. We are letting the wild things out. Some of them are harmless, some are beautiful, and some are terrifying. But they are all part of us, and to deny them is to deny a piece of ourselves. The writer who only writes with a plan is like a gardener who only plants a single row of tomatoes and then complains that the garden is boring. The gardener who writes freely—who lets the seeds fall where they may—will sometimes get weeds, but also sometimes get flowers that no one has ever seen before.

This brings me to a question that has haunted me for years: What is the relationship between freedom and discipline? In our culture, we often treat them as opposites. We think of the free spirit as the one who breaks rules, who improvises, who follows impulse. And we think of the disciplined person as the one who follows rules, who practices, who delays gratification. But I believe this is a false dichotomy. The greatest freedom is achieved through discipline, and the greatest discipline is a kind of freedom. Think of a musician who has practiced a piece for years, who knows every note, every dynamic, every breath. When they perform, they are free to express emotion, to shape the music in a way that is uniquely theirs. But that freedom is only possible because of the discipline that came before. The same is true of writing. If I have internalized the grammar and syntax of my language, if I have read widely and absorbed the rhythms of great prose, if I have written a thousand pages that will never see the light of day, then I am free to write something truly original. My mind is no longer encumbered by the mechanics of language; I have made them automatic, like breathing. And so I can focus on the deeper freedom, the freedom of thought, the freedom of imagination.

But there is a darker side to this coin. When I write freely, I sometimes worry that I am not being free at all—that I am merely repeating patterns that have been drilled into me by my education, my culture, my particular place in history. The river may feel free, but it is still flowing downhill, still following the path of least resistance. Is the same true of my thoughts? When I let my mind wander, am I truly wandering, or am I just retracing the same neural circuits, the same old grooves of anxiety and desire and habit? This is a question that cannot be answered easily. We are not transparent to ourselves. We do not have direct access to the machinery of our own minds. We only have the output, the words on the page, and even those are filtered through layers of interpretation and self-deception. Perhaps the best we can do is to keep writing, to keep making messes, to keep hoping that some of the messes will turn into gardens.

I want to turn now to something more concrete: the experience of walking. I am a walker, a flâneur of sorts, and I have found that walking is one of the best ways to free the mind. There is something about the rhythm of footsteps, the changing scenery, the gentle exertion of the body that allows thoughts to flow in ways they do not when I am sitting at a desk. I remember a walk I took last autumn, along a path that ran beside a small river. The leaves were turning, and the light was golden and low. I was not thinking about anything in particular—I was just feeling the air, listening to the water, watching the occasional duck paddle past. And then, out of nowhere, I had a memory of my childhood kitchen: the smell of my mother's bread, the sound of the radio playing old songs, the pattern of the wallpaper that I had not thought about in decades. The memory was so vivid that it stoped physical, a warmth in my chest. I stopped walking and just stood there, letting it wash over me. Where did that memory come from? I do not know. It was not triggered by anything I could identify. It was just there, a gift from the river of my own mind.

This is what I love about freedom in writing: it is a way of inviting those gifts, of making space for the unexpected. When I write without a plan, I am essentially walking through my own mind, hoping to stumble upon a memory, a phrase, an image that I did not know was there. Sometimes I do not. Sometimes I just walk through a barren landscape of tired words and dead metaphors. But sometimes, at the most improbable moments, I find something radiant, something that feels like it was waiting for me all along. And that feeling—that moment of discovery—is worth all the barren stretches in the world.

There is a philosophical dimension to all of this, and I cannot resist exploring it. The idea of free will, of the freedom to choose, is one of the oldest puzzles in human thought. We feel like we are free, but we also know that our choices are shaped by causes—by our genes, our upbringing, our environment, the state of our neurons at any given moment. Some philosophers have argued that free will is an illusion, that we are simply machines computing predetermined outputs. Others have argued that free will is real, that we are genuinely the authors of our actions. And still others have tried to find a middle path, suggesting that freedom is compatible with determinism, that we can be free even if our actions are caused. I am not going to solve that puzzle here. But I will say this: when I write, I feel free. Whether that feeling corresponds to some metaphysical reality, I cannot say. But it is a real feeling, and it has real consequences. When I feel free, I am more creative, more open, more willing to take risks. When I feel trapped, I am cautious, repetitive, boring. So perhaps the practical question is not "Are we free?" but "How can we cultivate the feeling of freedom?" And writing, I believe, is one of the best ways to do that.

But what about the reader? When I write freely, I am not just writing for myself. I am writing for someone else—someone who will pick up this essay and read these words, someone who may be sitting in a coffee shop or on a train or in a quiet room at night. I want that person to feel something, to be moved, to be entertained, to be challenged. But here is the paradox: if I write only for the reader, if I am constantly thinking about what they will think, I will not be free. The reader becomes a kind of jailer. And yet, if I write only for myself, if I ignore the reader entirely, I risk producing something solipsistic, something that no one else can understand or care about. The solution, I think, is to trust that the reader is a fellow human being, a fellow walker along the river. If I write truthfully, from the depths of my own experience, the reader will recognize something of their own experience in mine. The specifics may differ, but the underlying emotions—the joy, the fear, the confusion, the wonder—are universal. The river of my mind flows into the river of theirs, and for a moment, we are connected.

This connection is one of the most beautiful things about writing. It is a way of reaching across time and space, of touching someone you have never met. I think about the authors I have loved, the ones who have shaped my thinking and my feeling. I never met them. I will never meet most of them. And yet, I feel like I know them. I feel like they have spoken directly to me, across the decades, across the miles. That is the power of written language: it is a vessel for consciousness, a way of preserving the soul's wanderings so that others can wander through them too. When I write freely, I am not just making a mess; I am making a gift. A messy gift, perhaps, but a gift nonetheless.

I want to think now about the relationship between freedom and memory. Our memories are not like files on a computer, stored intact and retrievable at will. They are more like rivers, constantly shifting and reshaping themselves, merging with other rivers, eroding their banks. Every time we remember something, we are not playing back a recording; we are reconstructing the event, filling in the gaps, changing the details. This is why two people can remember the same event differently, and why our own memories of childhood can feel so strange and fragmented. Memory is a creative act, and it is a kind of writing. When we remember, we are telling ourselves a story about the past, and that story is always a little bit fictional. The freedom to write is also the freedom to remember—not in the sense of changing the facts, but in the sense of giving the past meaning, of weaving it into a narrative that makes sense of who we are.

I have been thinking about a specific memory: the summer I turned twelve, when my family took a trip to the mountains. I remember the cabin we stayed in, with its wood-paneled walls and the smell of pine. I remember the lake, cold and clear, and the way the sunlight sparkled on the surface. I remember catching my first fish, a small rainbow trout that I was both proud of and a little sad about. I remember my father laughing, my mother taking photographs, the sound of a loon calling across the water at dusk. It was a good summer, a golden summer. Or was it? I do not really know. I know that there were also arguments, and rain, and a long car ride that made us all grumpy. But those details have faded. What remains is a warm glow, a sense of peace that may or may not have been there. I have rewritten that summer many times, in my head and on the page. Every retelling is a little different. But the essential feeling—the feeling of being loved, of being safe, of being at home in the world—that has remained constant. Perhaps that is what memory is for: not to give us an accurate record, but to give us a sense of continuity, a story we can live by.

There is a dark side to this too. We can also rewrite our memories in ways that are harmful. We can dwell on the past, replaying the same scenes of hurt and humiliation, turning them into a prison. We can become trapped in a narrative of victimhood or guilt. Freedom, in this context, means being able to step outside that narrative, to see it as a story that we are telling and to tell a different story instead. This is not easy. It takes discipline, and it takes courage. But it is possible. Writing can help. When we write about our traumas, our failures, our fears, we are taking control of the narrative. We are moving from being a character in a story to being the author. I have found this to be true in my own life, in the quiet hours I have spent journaling about things that were painful to remember. The writing did not erase the pain, but it changed its shape. It made it manageable. It made it mine.

And so I circle back to the blank page, to the silence and the hum. I have been writing for a while now, and I have no idea if this essay is any good. I have not planned it, have not outlined it, have not revised it. I have simply let the words flow, and I have tried to keep up. There have been moments when the flow has felt effortless, when the sentences have seemed to write themselves. There have been other moments when I have had to pause, to search for the next word, to fight the urge to go back and fix something I thought was clumsy. But I have kept going, because that is the discipline of free writing: you keep going, you do not stop, you trust that the river will carry you.

And now, as I approach what feels like a natural end, I want to reflect on what this experience has taught me. It has taught me that freedom is not a destination but a practice. It is not something you have or do not have; it is something you do, again and again, in small ways and large. It is the decision to write the sentence you are afraid to write. It is the decision to tell the truth when a lie would be easier. It is the decision to open yourself to the unknown, to let go of control, to trust that the universe—or your own unconscious, or whatever you want to call it—has something to offer you. It is not always comfortable. It is not always productive. But it is always alive.

There is a line from the poet Rainer Maria Rilke that has stayed with me for years. In *Letters to a Young Poet*, he writes: "Be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart and try to love the questions themselves." I think this is the essence of free writing. It is a way of loving the questions, of living in the uncertainty, of refusing to close off possibilities too soon. The blank page is a question. The first word is an answer, but it is only the first of many, and the answer is never final. We are always writing, always revising, always exploring. That is the human condition. That is the gift of language. And that is why I will keep writing, freely, for as long as I can.

I look out the window now, and I see the sky has darkened. Rain is beginning to fall, and the drops are tapping against the glass. It is a gentle sound, a sound like a hundred tiny rivers running down the pane. I think about all the rivers of the world, the ones I have seen and the ones I will never see. They all flow to the sea, and the sea is the same sea, the one ocean that touches every shore. Perhaps our thoughts are like that too. Every free thought, every wild idea, every moment of genuine creativity flows into the great ocean of human consciousness. We are not separate. We are all part of the same water. And when I write, I am adding my drop to that ocean, joining a conversation that has been going on for millennia. It is a humbling thought, but also a comforting one. I am alone in this room, but I am not alone. I am surrounded by the voices of all the writers who have come before me, and I am speaking to the voices of all who will come after. That is the freedom of writing: it is a way of being with others, even when we are by ourselves.

So let me end where I began, with the silence and the hum. The hum is still there, even now, beneath the sound of the rain. It is the sound of possibility, of the next sentence, the next page, the next river bend. I do not know what I will write tomorrow, or the day after, or the year after that. But I know that I will write. I will keep putting words on the page, keep making messes, keep searching for the gold flakes in the silt. And if you are reading this, I hope you will do the same. Not because you have to. Not because it will make you famous or rich or wise. But because it is a way of being free, and freedom is the only thing worth living for. Write freely. Let the river carry you. Trust that it knows where it is going, even if you do not.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
“Write freely about whatever you want.” It is a deceptively simple instruction. No topic, no constraints, no brief. Just a blank space and a blinking cursor, waiting for me to fill it with something worthwhile. But freedom has a strange way of making the mind feel heavier than any deadline ever could. The moment you can write about anything, the temptation is to write about everything, or worse, to write about nothing at all. So perhaps the best way to begin is not with a grand thesis or a carefully constructed argument, but with a confession: I have no idea what I am about to write. And that, I think, is exactly the right place to start.

We spend most of our lives being told what to do. Our calendars are packed with obligations, our conversations are filtered through expectations, and our thoughts are often shaped by the invisible hand of convention. Even in the supposedly creative spaces of our lives, we are usually responding to a prompt, a problem, a product requirement, or a social cue. There is nothing wrong with that, of course. Constraints can be liberating. A sonnet is a cage, but the cage is what gives the sonnet its shape. A chess board is a set of rules, but the rules are what make the game infinite. Yet there is something uniquely valuable in the act of wandering without a map, of letting the mind drift to places it would never go if it had to produce something useful. Free writing is not a luxury; it is a kind of mental hygiene.

I remember a professor I had in college who began every seminar by asking us to write for ten minutes, completely without stopping, about whatever came into our heads. She called it “morning pages,” although we did it in the afternoon. At first I hated it. My hand would cramp, my sentences would trail off, and I would fill entire pages with apologies for having nothing to say. But after a few weeks, something shifted. The writing became less about producing something good and more about clearing away the noise. It was like sweeping a dusty room. You do not sweep because you expect to find treasure; you sweep because you need to see the floor. Once the floor was visible, the actual work of the seminar felt easier. My ideas were sharper because they had room to move. My voice was clearer because it had been exercised without judgment.

That is the paradox of free writing: it is the most private, least performative act, and yet it is the thing that makes public writing possible. When we write for an audience, we are constantly editing, hedging, and anticipating reactions. We ask ourselves: Will this sound smart? Will this offend anyone? Is this too long? Is this too short? These are useful questions, but if we ask them too early, they strangle the thought before it has a chance to breathe. Free writing is a way of postponing the editor, of letting the raw material pile up on the page so that we can later shape it into something intentional. It is the difference between building a house and drawing an architectural blueprint. You cannot draw a blueprint for a house you have not imagined, and you cannot imagine a house without first playing with piles of bricks.

I have been thinking a lot about attention lately. Not in the abstract, philosophical sense, but in the very concrete sense of why I cannot seem to read a novel for more than ten minutes without reaching for my phone. There is a whole industry devoted to capturing our attention, and it is very good at its job. The notifications, the infinite scroll, the autoplay videos, the red badges—all of these are designed to exploit a quirk of human psychology: we crave novelty, and we are terrified of missing something. But the cost of constantly refreshing our attention is that we forget what it feels like to be bored, and boredom, it turns out, is one of the most fertile states for the mind. When you are bored, you start to notice things. You start to follow threads that were always there but were too quiet to be heard. You start to think in a different way, not in the linear, task-oriented way of checking items off a list, but in the looping, associative way that leads to unexpected connections.

I recently tried an experiment. I left my phone in another room for an entire afternoon, and I sat in a chair by the window with no book, no notebook, and no plan.
